summary: Dominica waives visas for around a hundred nationalities, including the US, Canada, the UK, the EU and most Commonwealth countries — immigration normally stamps a short stay on arrival that can be extended up to six months — while CARICOM nationals move freely and everyone else applies for a visa in advance.

passportValidity.text: Travel with a passport valid for at least six months on arrival. Shorter validity is sometimes accepted for visa-free visitors, but airlines apply the six-month rule at check-in.

vaccinations.name: Yellow fever
vaccinations.text: A yellow fever vaccination certificate is required from travelers aged one year and over arriving from — or having recently transited — a country with risk of yellow fever transmission. No vaccination is required if you fly in directly from Europe, North America or the rest of the Caribbean.

source.name: Government of the Commonwealth of Dominica

travelInsurance.text: Insurance is not an entry condition, but Dominica's hospital is small and serious cases are flown to Martinique, Guadeloupe or Barbados — cover including medical evacuation matters more here than on larger islands, especially for hikers and divers.

source.name: Government of the Commonwealth of Dominica

onwardTicket.text: Visitors must show a return or onward ticket and give the address where they are staying; the officer sets the length of stay from those details.

source.name: Government of the Commonwealth of Dominica

proofOfFunds.text: No fixed amount is published. Officers may ask how you will support yourself if you request a long stay or arrive without confirmed accommodation.

source.name: Government of the Commonwealth of Dominica

declarations.name: Immigration and customs declaration
declarations.text: Arriving passengers complete an immigration and customs declaration card, handed out on the flight or at the terminal. Dominica has been trialling an online version. Use it if your airline or the Immigration Division points you to one.

source.name: Government of the Commonwealth of Dominica

currencyLimits.text: Cash or bearer instruments worth XCD 10,000 or more (roughly USD 3,700) must be declared to customs on arrival and departure.

source.name: Government of the Commonwealth of Dominica

notes: Firearms, ammunition and spear guns require a permit — this catches out yacht crews in particular.
Plants, soil, fresh produce, meat and dairy are restricted to protect Dominica's agriculture; clean hiking boots before you travel.
Drones must be declared and may need permission before being flown, especially near the national parks.

payments.text: Cards work in Roseau hotels, larger restaurants and supermarkets, but much of the island — village guesthouses, guides, minibuses, market stalls — is cash only. Carry East Caribbean dollars; US dollars are accepted but change comes back in EC$.

safety.text: Dominica has low crime and a strong community feel. The real hazards are natural: flash floods, landslides after heavy rain, powerful river currents and remote hiking trails with no phone signal. The island is also directly in the hurricane belt.

source.name: U.S. Department of State — Dominica Travel Advisory

bestTimeToVisit.text: December to April is drier and best for hiking the Waitukubuli National Trail. Dominica is the greenest island in the Caribbean because it rains a lot. Expect showers year-round, and hurricanes between June and November.

tips.text: Dominica is not the Dominican Republic. They are different countries with different entry rules, currencies and airports. Check that flights, insurance and visas name the Commonwealth of Dominica (airport codes DOM and DCF) before you book.

There are few long-haul flights: most visitors connect through Antigua, Barbados, St Lucia or Guadeloupe, or take the ferry from the French islands. Douglas–Charles airport has limited late-day operations, so build in a connection buffer.
Visitors must buy a local driving permit (around EC$30–40) to drive, issued by car rental firms. Roads are steep, narrow and winding, and driving is on the left.
Rain changes rivers fast. Do not cross swollen rivers or hike alone on the Waitukubuli trail during heavy weather, and check trail conditions locally — sections still change after storm damage.

faq.question: Do I need a visa for Dominica?
faq.answer: Most visitors do not. Citizens of the United States, Canada, the United Kingdom, the EU and most Commonwealth countries enter without a visa, and CARICOM nationals move freely. If your nationality is not exempt, apply for a visitor visa to a Dominica high commission, embassy or honorary consulate before traveling.

faq.question: How long can I stay in Dominica?
faq.answer: The immigration officer decides on arrival and often stamps a short initial stay — commonly around three weeks — based on your ticket and accommodation. Extensions are granted by the Immigration Division in Roseau up to a maximum of six months, so ask for the time you actually need at the desk.

faq.question: Is Dominica the same as the Dominican Republic?
faq.answer: No. Dominica is a small English-speaking island in the eastern Caribbean; the Dominican Republic is a much larger Spanish-speaking country sharing Hispaniola with Haiti. Their visa rules are completely separate. Make sure you are reading the right one.

faq.question: Do I need a return ticket for Dominica?
faq.answer: Yes. Visitors are expected to hold a confirmed onward or return ticket and to give the address where they will stay. Both are commonly asked for at immigration.

faq.question: Can I work remotely from Dominica?
faq.answer: Yes. The Work In Nature (WIN) extended stay visa lets remote workers and their families live in Dominica for up to 18 months, for a fee of roughly USD 800 for a single applicant. It requires income earned outside Dominica and valid health insurance; a normal visitor stamp does not allow you to work locally.
